# Water-powered trip hammer and stamp mill (`trip_hammer_water_powered`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs water_wheel, cam_camshaft; helped by bloomery_iron
- Core idea: Cams on the shaft of a water wheel press down the tail or lift the head of a pivoted hammer beam and let it fall, 60 to 150 blows a minute, tirelessly. The same motion with vertical stamps crushes ore, pounds rags to paper pulp, hulls rice, fulls woollen cloth and beats flax. In the forge a heavy helve hammer (100 to 300 kg) works blooms of iron into bars, a lighter fast one draws them out. The hammer head, anvil block and the pivot take the punishment; the anvil needs a deep foundation of timber or stone.
- Pitfalls:
  - A weak pivot or a shallow anvil foundation: the hammer shakes the building apart
  - Cams that strike the beam instead of sliding under it
  - No way to stop the hammer quickly while the wheel runs (prop or sluice)
- History: china: 1st c. BC – foot-worked tilt hammer; c. 20 AD water-powered (Huan Tan, Xin lun); rows of hammers on one shaft by the 3rd c.; rome: 1st–2nd c. AD – water-driven pestles in Italy (Pliny, reading debated) and ore stamps at mines in Spain and at Dolaucothi, Wales; islamic: by the 10th–11th c. – water-driven stamps for paper pulp, rice and ore (extent debated); europe: late 11th c. – fulling mills in Normandy; 12th–13th c. forge hammers, spread by Cistercian houses; c. 1280 paper stamp mills at Fabriano
- Read:
  - Adam Lucas, Wind, Water, Work: Ancient and Medieval Milling Technology (2006)
  - Georgius Agricola, De re metallica (1556; tr. H. C. Hoover & L. H. Hoover, 1912)
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
